title: The Rochdale Pioneers
text:
In the 1840s Rochdale, a mill town near Manchester, was suffering. Flannel weavers had lost a strike, wages were low, and shopkeepers often sold adulterated food at high prices and on credit that trapped families in debt. Earlier attempts at cooperative shops in Britain had mostly failed.

A group of working men, many of them weavers, formed the Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers. Over most of a year they saved a pound each, a large sum for them, some paying in a few pence a week. With the small capital that resulted, on 21 December 1844 they opened a shop on Toad Lane with a meager stock of butter, sugar, flour, oatmeal and candles. Local accounts say boys jeered at them through the window.

What made the Rochdale Pioneers different was their set of rules. Membership was open to anyone. Each member had one vote, regardless of how much capital he held. Goods were sold for cash only, at market prices, and were pure and honestly weighed. Profits were returned to members in proportion to how much they had bought. Part of the surplus was set aside for education.

The shop survived and grew. Within a few decades the society had many branches and thousands of members, and its rules, known as the Rochdale Principles, became the model for the cooperative movement around the world.
lesson: Ordinary people who pool their resources under fair, clear rules can build something lasting. Good rules matter as much as good intentions.
source: George Jacob Holyoake, The History of the Rochdale Pioneers (1857)
